body:
In the second user study session, P2 clicked a file in the file explorer and expected the dependency map to move to it, but nothing happened. They weren't sure whether the explorer and the map were linked at all.

`DependencyMap.tsx` already centers the map on the selected file, but only when that file has its own node. When the file's module is collapsed (the default on most repos), `flow.getInternalNode(fileNodeId(selectedPath))` returns `undefined` and the effect exits early. The collapsed module does get highlighted, but the map doesn't pan to it, so the highlight is often off-screen.

Related: #92, whose scope includes "selecting a file anywhere in the workspace pans the map to it". This issue covers the case where the selected file sits inside a collapsed module.

## Scope
- When a file is selected from the explorer, the reading list, or the detail panel and its module is collapsed, expand that module (and its parents) so the file gets its own node, then center on it.
- If expanding would make the graph too big, center on the collapsed module instead and show a short hint such as "Inside `app/` (collapsed). Expand to see the file."
- Keep the zoom level steady when the map pans, like the existing `setCenter` call does.
- Selecting the same file again should still re-center the map, even if the user has panned away.

## Done when
- [ ] Selecting a file inside a collapsed module in the explorer centers the map on that file
- [ ] `DependencyMap.test.tsx` covers centering on a file inside a collapsed module
- [ ] `Workspace` test covers clicking a file in the explorer and checking that the map reacts
- [ ] Checked by hand on the bookshop fixture and the 1,000-file benchmark repo (#45)
title: Selecting a file in the explorer should move the map to it, even inside a collapsed module

body:
In the second user study session, P2 couldn't tell which way a dependency went on the map. Many arrows cross over each other, and the arrowheads are small, so it was hard to see whether a file imports another file or is imported by it. This slowed down the "trace what a feature depends on" task the most: P2 spent about 6 of their 10 minutes on it and missed two dependencies.

Right now every edge is drawn the same way (`mapLayout.ts` gives each one a 16px `ArrowClosed` marker and the same muted stroke), and the only explanation is the toolbar line "Arrows point from a file to what it imports." When a file is selected, every edge that touches it turns the same accent color, whether it goes in or out.

Related: #92 (decluttering map navigation and controls) and #81 (architecture/feature/focus/search views). This issue covers **which way edges point and how easy they are to follow**.

## Scope
- When a file or module is selected, color its outgoing edges ("imports") and incoming edges ("imported by") differently, and dim everything else.
- Make the arrowheads bigger and easier to see at the default zoom.
- Cut down on crossing edges: tune the layout direction and spacing in `layoutMap`, and route edges so they don't run through nodes.
- Replace the single toolbar sentence with a small legend that shows both edge colors.
- Optional: add "Imports" and "Imported by" counts to the detail panel, so users can check the map against a list.

## Done when
- [ ] With a file selected, the imports and imported-by edges are different colors, and the legend explains them
- [ ] Arrowheads can be seen at the default zoom on the bookshop fixture
- [ ] `mapLayout.test.ts` covers the direction classes on edges around a selection
- [ ] `DependencyMap.test.tsx` covers the legend
- [ ] Checked by hand on the 1,000-file benchmark repo (#45) for fewer crossings
title: Make dependency direction clear on the map: in/out edge colors, bigger arrows, fewer crossings

body:
Users don't know what the search box does. They can't tell if it searches file names, symbols, or text, what makes a file rank higher, or why a query returns nothing. The only hint is one landing-page line ("Type a word like 'login' or a function name").

## Scope
Explain search in-app, either as a first-use pop-up on the search bar or as a step in the first-run tutorial (#91). Cover:
- **What is searched**: file paths, module-level symbols (functions and classes), import names, plus docstrings, comments, and class members (#77, part 1). Update this text when hybrid/embedding search lands (#77, part 2).
- **How results are ranked**: matches are weighted by where they occur (name vs. docstring vs. comment), and files that other matches depend on rank higher.
- **What the order means**: the results are a suggested *reading* order with dependencies first, not the order the code runs in. See #93.
- **Tips**: try a feature word ("checkout"), a function or class name, or a module name. What to do when there are no results.
- A small "?" / "How search works" link next to the search bar reopens the explanation.
- Remember per viewer that the pop-up was seen (`localStorage` in try/catch).

## Done when
- [ ] The pop-up (or tutorial step) shows on the first search and can be dismissed
- [ ] "How search works" reopens it at any time
- [ ] The text matches what `SearchService` actually indexes and ranks on
- [ ] Vitest covers show, dismiss, and reopen
title: Explain how search works in a first-use pop-up or the tutorial

body:
The reading list shows a reason for each file, but it only explains **why the file matched** ("Matches …; depended on by N other matching file(s)"). It never explains **why the file sits at its position** in the suggested order. Users see `#3 of 8` and can't tell why it comes before `#4`.

The order comes from `SearchService._reading_order` (`backend/repolens/search/service.py`). It is a Kahn topological sort over the matching files' imports: dependencies come first, ties are broken by score, and cycles are broken by picking the lowest remaining file. All the information needed to explain it is already there.

Related: #36 (reading path recommendations), #82 (Read first / Edit here / Tests to run), and #79 (guided tour step reasons).

## Scope
- The backend adds an `orderReason` to each `RankedFile` (alongside the existing match `reason`), for example:
  - "Read first: `cart.py` and `pricing.py` import it."
  - "Comes after `models.py`, which it imports."
  - "No dependencies among the results; ranked by match score."
  - "Part of an import cycle with `a.py`; placed here to break the cycle."
- Add `orderReason` to `frontend/src/api/types.ts` and the mock client.
- Show it in `ReadingList.tsx` under each entry, and in the "Reading order" section of `FileDetailPanel.tsx`.

## Done when
- [ ] Bookshop e2e fixture: hand-written expected order reasons in `expected.json` match
- [ ] `test_api_contract.py` covers `orderReason`
- [ ] A unit test covers the cycle-break reason
- [ ] Vitest covers the order reason in the reading list and the detail panel
title: Explain why each file is placed where it is in the suggested reading order

body:
The dependency map's navigation is cluttered. The toolbar (Reset view, Collapse all), the React Flow zoom controls, and the background grid compete for space, and on mid-size repos it's hard to move around and keep your place.

Related: #80 (hide tests/tools/docs by default) and #81 (architecture/feature/focus/search views) reduce **how many nodes** are drawn. This issue covers the **navigation controls and interaction** around the map.

## Scope
- Group the map controls into one compact toolbar: zoom in/out, fit, reset, collapse all. Drop the duplicate controls.
- Make the background grid lighter or remove it.
- Keep the selected file and search matches in view: when a file is selected from the sidebar, reading list, or detail panel, pan to it without changing the zoom level unexpectedly.
- Add a small "you are here" cue, such as a breadcrumb of the expanded module path, so users know which part of the repo they are viewing.
- Consider a minimap that is collapsed by default for large graphs.
- Keyboard: arrow keys pan, `+`/`-` zoom, `0` fits, without stealing focus from the search bar.

## Done when
- [ ] One toolbar holds every map control, with no duplicates
- [ ] Selecting a file anywhere in the workspace pans the map to it
- [ ] `DependencyMap.test.tsx` covers the toolbar actions and pan-to-selection
- [ ] Checked by hand on the 1,000-file benchmark repo (#45)
title: Declutter dependency map navigation and controls

body:
New users don't know where to start once an analysis loads. The landing page explains three steps, but the workspace then shows the search bar, sidebar tabs, dependency map, and detail panel all at once, with no guidance.

Related: #79 adds an **Overview** tab and a guided tour of the *repository* (entry points, core files). This issue covers the *app*: a tutorial on how to use RepoLens, and a simpler first screen.

## Scope
- **First-run tutorial**: a short, skippable walkthrough of the workspace, 4–5 steps, each highlighting one area:
  - search bar
  - sidebar (Files / Reading order)
  - dependency map
  - file detail panel and "Next in reading order"
- A **Help / "Show tutorial again"** button in the workspace header.
- Remember per viewer that the tutorial was seen (`localStorage`, wrapped in try/catch so the page still works without it).
- **Simplify the home/landing page**: trim the "How it works" and "What this version supports" text so the repo URL input is the clear focus. Move details behind a "Learn more" disclosure or into the tutorial.
- **Simplify the first workspace view**: show only what a new user needs first, e.g. collapse the detail panel until a file is selected, or start on #79's Overview tab once it lands.

## Done when
- [ ] The tutorial shows on the first visit to a completed analysis and not again after it is finished or skipped
- [ ] The tutorial can be reopened from the workspace
- [ ] The landing page fits above the fold on a 1366×768 screen with the URL input focused
- [ ] Vitest covers tutorial show/skip/reopen and the persisted "seen" state
title: Add a first-run tutorial and simplify the home and workspace UI

`LanguageAnalyzer` already isolates parsing. The import classifier and the pipeline runner are still Python-only.

body:
From TA feedback (Assignment 3): cache where it actually saves time. A developer onboarding onto one codebase opens the same repo again and again across sessions, so caching on their side makes sense, possibly in layers: keep the parts of the graph they revisit on their machine, and keep the analyzed repo on the backend so nothing gets rescanned.

## Scope
- **Backend**
  - A persistent database (from the Docker/CD issue), so a restart doesn't force rescans.
  - In-flight de-duplication in `PipelineAnalysisRunner.start`: two requests for the same `(repo, sha)` share one queued or running analysis.
  - `ETag` and `Cache-Control: private, immutable` on `/graph`, `/files/…` and `/overview`, which never change for a given analysis id.
- **Client**
  - A "Recent repositories" list on the landing page.
  - For each repo, remember the last selected file, feature area, expanded modules and filters in `localStorage`, so a returning developer lands where they left off.
  - Optional: cache the graph and overview in IndexedDB, keyed by `(repoUrl, sha)`, until `expiresAt`.

## Done when
- [ ] Test: two concurrent `POST /analyses` for the same repo trigger only one download
- [ ] Test: a second `GET /graph` with `If-None-Match` returns 304
- [ ] Vitest covers recent repos and restored view state, and a storage failure doesn't break the page

Schedule: **week 3**.
title: Cache in layers: dedupe in-flight analyses, HTTP ETags, recent repos on the client

body:
From TA feedback (Assignment 2): *the restriction to GitHub stands out. Most features apply to any Git-compatible repository, so if I gave it a GitLab link I'd expect it to work.*

## Scope
- `ingestion/urls.py`: parse URLs into a host-neutral `RepoLocation(host, path)` that allows GitLab nested groups. Remove the duplicate `api/app.py:validate_github_repo_url`.
- Add a `RefResolver` Protocol to `ingestion/ports.py`. The `RepoSource` port already names GitLab as its second implementation.
- **GitLab**: `GitLabRefResolver` (`/api/v4/projects/{id}/repository/commits/{ref}`) and `GitLabSource` (`/repository/archive.zip?sha=`). Both go through the existing `HttpsArchiveFetcher`, with GitLab hosts added to the allowlist.
- **Any public https git URL**: resolve with `git ls-remote`, then fetch with a hardened shallow `GitCloneSource`:
  - `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` and `GIT_LFS_SKIP_SMUDGE=1`
  - `-c protocol.allow=never -c protocol.https.allow=always`
  - `core.hooksPath=/dev/null`
  - no submodules, a timeout, and a size check against `ArchiveLimits` after cloning
- **Source links per host**, replacing `build_github_source_url`. Generic hosts hide the link.
- **Frontend**: `utils/repoInput.ts` accepts any https git URL, and "Open source on GitHub" becomes "Open source".
- **README**: stop saying "GitHub only".

## Done when
- [ ] Unit tests cover URL parsing for each host and the exact clone arguments and environment
- [ ] Manual check: a public gitlab.com Python repo and one generic https git repo both analyze end to end in the Docker image

Schedule: **week 3**.
title: Accept GitLab and any public https git URL, not just GitHub

body:
From TA feedback (Assignment 5): the beta "does exactly what it says on the tin". It shows imports and symbols, but it doesn't onboard anyone yet. In-class feedback (11/5) also asked us to **show architecture**, **tailor for new users**, and **split the map by feature**.

## Scope
New backend package `repolens/onboarding/`, computed from the stored graph in a new pipeline stage `summarizing`:

- **File categories**: `source | test | tool | docs | example | config | migration`, decided from path and name heuristics (`tests/`, `test_*.py`, `*_test.py`, `conftest.py`, `scripts/`, `tools/`, `examples/`, `docs/`, `setup.py`, `noxfile.py`, `migrations/`). New `files.category` column. The filters and task-mode issues need this.
- **Entry points**, detected from analyzer markers:
  - `if __name__ == "__main__"`, `__main__.py`, `manage.py`
  - module-level `FastAPI()`, `Flask()` and `typer.Typer()` objects, and `@click.command` / `@app.route` decorators
  - `[project.scripts]` in `pyproject.toml`, read with `tomllib` and never executed
- **Core files**: PageRank or in-degree over internal import edges.
- **Architecture**: a package-level graph, plus layers by topological depth (foundations → services → entry points). Report cycles.
- **Feature areas**: community detection (label propagation) on the import graph. Name each area from its most frequent path and symbol tokens.
- **Guided tour**: a whole-repo reading order of 8–12 files, from an entry point to the core files it reaches, with dependencies first. It reuses the Kahn ordering in `SearchService._reading_order`, lifted into a shared helper. Each step gets a one-line reason.
- **File summaries**: the first line of the module docstring; failing that, a generated line like "Defines 3 classes, 5 functions; used by 7 files".
- **API**: `GET /analyses/{id}/overview` returns `{entryPoints, coreFiles, architecture{packages, edges, layers}, areas[], tour[]}`. Add it to `frontend/src/api/types.ts` and the mock client.
- **Frontend**: a new default **Overview** tab in `Workspace.tsx` with:
  - an architecture strip
  - the entry points
  - "Start the tour", which reuses the Next action in `FileDetailPanel`
  - the feature-area list, where clicking an area scopes the map

## Done when
- [ ] The bookshop e2e fixture's `expected.json` (hand-written) gains entry points (`manage.py`, `bookshop/app.py`), categories, and tour expectations, and the e2e test passes
- [ ] `test_api_contract.py` covers `/overview`
- [ ] The Overview tab has Vitest coverage and is the first thing shown when an analysis completes

Depends on the docstring/comment extraction issue (needed for summaries). Schedule: **week 2**.

body:
From TA feedback (Assignment 5 and 11/5): search only matches exact keywords. A new hire asks something vague, like *"if I'm meant to work on prod, where do I start?"* If nothing in the repo is literally called "prod", RepoLens returns nothing.

Decision: **a local embedding model, combined with the existing keyword scoring**. It needs no API key, works offline, and ships in the Docker image.

## Scope
1. **Richer extraction** (week 1; closes step 1 of #74 and the indexing half of #44): module, class and function docstrings, comments (read with `tokenize`, nothing executed), methods, and class-level fields. Fill the `comments` table, which exists but is always empty, and add docstrings to the index.
2. **`Embedder` port** in `search/embedding.py`:
   - `FastEmbedEmbedder`: `fastembed` running the ONNX model `BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5` (~67 MB, CPU only).
   - `HashEmbedder`: deterministic, for tests and CI. Tests never download a model.
3. **`indexing` pipeline stage**:
   - One chunk per file: path words split on snake/camel case, module docstring, symbols, docstrings and comments. Large files also get one chunk per symbol.
   - Vectors go in a new `embeddings` table.
   - Search is brute-force cosine similarity in numpy; up to 1,000 files doesn't need a vector database.
4. **Hybrid ranking**: combine the keyword and semantic scores with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, then apply the existing dependencies-first reading order. Drop stop-words from keyword terms, and send "where do I start" / "overview" queries to the onboarding tour.
5. **Evaluation**: add a `RepoLens-hybrid` column to `benchmarks/search_precision.py`. Add vague natural-language queries to `labeled_queries.json`, labeled *before* running, following the existing labeling rule.
6. **Frontend**: change the SearchBar prompt to "Describe what you want to work on…". Add a `semantic` match kind to `ReadingList` that shows the docstring or comment snippet that matched.

## Done when
- [ ] The 4 queries that return nothing in `measured_precision.json` return labeled files
- [ ] Hybrid precision@5 is at least the keyword score on every query, and the refreshed numbers are committed with an explanation
- [ ] The e2e test includes a natural-language query

Related: #74, #44, #37 / PR #67. Schedule: extraction in **week 1**, embeddings and benchmark in **week 2**.
title: Index docstrings, comments, and methods, then add local-embedding hybrid search

body:
From TA feedback (Assignments 4 and 5, and 11/5):
- `make` comes with build-essential, which many systems don't have; the TA's fresh Ubuntu VM didn't. `venv` isn't always installed either. A new developer, the person RepoLens is for, can't be expected to know these workarounds.
- *Streamline this significantly for the final release: use CD, lock down the environment, pin versions/dependencies.* The TA recommended Docker.
- Testing on 3.11, 3.12 and 3.13 adds little; pick one known-good version and pin it. Say "Python 3.11 and up" rather than listing versions.

## Scope
- **Single image** from a multi-stage root `Dockerfile`:
  - A `node:22` stage builds `frontend/dist`.
  - A `python:3.12-slim-bookworm` stage (exact tag) runs the backend as a non-root user, with locked dependencies and `git`.
  - FastAPI serves the API under `/api` and the built frontend as static files, so production needs no `*` CORS rule.
- **Persistent SQLite** at `REPOLENS_DB_PATH`; tests keep the in-memory default. Recreate the database when the schema version changes, since it is only a 24-hour cache. Add `GET /api/health`.
- **`docker-compose.yml`**: port 8000 and a `/data` volume.
- **Pinning**: `uv` with `backend/uv.lock`, `.python-version` and `.nvmrc`. Developers without Docker run `uv sync` and `npm ci`; uv installs Python itself, so no system venv is needed. The Makefile stays as an optional shortcut.
- **CI**: run the main backend suite on the pinned 3.12 only. A small compatibility job on 3.11 (the minimum) and the newest Python backs up "3.11 and up".
- **CD** (`release.yml`, on push to `main`):
  1. Build the image.
  2. Smoke-test it: `/api/health`, and the e2e suite inside the container.
  3. Push to GHCR as `:sha` and `:latest`.
  4. Trigger the host's deploy hook (Render or Fly.io, stored as a secret) when one is configured.

## Done when
- [ ] On a fresh Ubuntu VM with only Docker installed (no build-essential, no venv), `docker compose up` serves RepoLens on `:8000` and analyzes a public repo
- [ ] The release workflow passes on `main` and the image is published to GHCR
- [ ] The hosted URL works and is at the top of the README (together with the docs issue, this closes #49)

Advances #48 and #49. Schedule: **week 1**.
title: Package RepoLens as one Docker image with pinned deps, persistent cache, and CD

body:
Found by the hand-labeled accuracy fixtures in #34 (PR #71). This is the one recorded miss in that measurement — **84/85 references correct, 98.8%** — and it is deliberately left failing so it does not get lost.

## Problem

When a module file and a package directory share a name, the file wins in CPython and the directory becomes unreachable. The classifier resolves through the directory anyway.

Fixture: `backend/tests/fixtures/import_classification/module_directory_collision/`

```
repo/app/config.py          <- module file
repo/app/config/defaults.py <- directory of the same name, unreachable
```

For `import app.config.defaults`:

| | Result |
|---|---|
| CPython | `ModuleNotFoundError` — `app.config` resolves to `app/config.py`, which is not a package, so it cannot contain `defaults` |
| RepoLens | internal edge to `app/config/defaults.py` |
| Correct label | `unresolved` |

## Impact

A wrong internal edge, which is the failure mode we have agreed is worse than an honest gap: it silently adds a dependency to the map that Python would never take, and the file detail panel shows an importer relationship that does not exist. An `unresolved` label would be correct and harmless here.

Scope is narrow — it needs a module file and a directory of the same name in the same parent — but it is not contrived; it happens when a module grows into a package and the old file is left behind.

Note the sibling case **does** work: `app/models.py` alongside `app/models/` with `app/models/__init__.py` present classifies correctly, because the directory is a real package. The bug is specific to the shadowed, non-package directory.

## Suggested fix

In `backend/repolens/analysis/classifier.py`, when a dotted path resolves to a module *file*, stop — do not continue descending into a same-named directory. The base-resolves-before-submodule ordering from #27 is already in place; this is the adjacent case where the base resolves to a file and the remaining segments therefore cannot resolve at all.

## Heads-up for whoever fixes this

The #34 measurement is a **snapshot test**. `backend/tests/test_import_classification.py` pins the current numbers against `backend/benchmarks/measured_classification.json`, including this miss:

- `test_the_measurement_reproduces_the_recorded_numbers`
- `test_overall_accuracy_is_84_of_85_references`

Fixing the classifier **will fail those two tests until the recorded numbers are regenerated**. That is intended — it is a change detector, not a regression. Update `measured_classification.json` and the `84 of 85` expectation as part of the fix. The `module_directory_collision` layout should go from 10/11 (90.9%) to 11/11, and overall from 84/85 to 85/85.

Labels in the fixtures were verified against CPython `importlib`, not read back from the classifier, so the expected answer here is trustworthy.
title: Classifier resolves import through a directory shadowed by a same-named module file

body:
Follow-up from the measurement landed in #37 (PR #67). Filing while the numbers are fresh.

## What #37 measured

Top-5 precision over 19 hand-labeled queries across 3 fixture repos:

| System | Top-5 precision |
|---|---|
| **RepoLens** | **0.211** |
| grep (filename baseline) | 0.042 |
| grep + ranking | 0.053 |
| ideal ceiling | 0.326 |

RepoLens wins on all 3 repos and is not beaten on any individual query, so the premise holds: structured search beats grepping filenames.

## The problem the measurement exposed

The interesting finding is *how* RepoLens falls short of the 0.326 ceiling:

- **All 11 labeled files RepoLens misses are recall failures, not ranking failures.** The ranker is not putting the right file low; the right file is not in the index at all.
- **4 of the 19 queries return nothing whatsoever.**

The index currently holds only:
- file path
- module-level symbols
- import `raw_name`s

So a query matching a term that appears only inside a function body, in a docstring, or in a comment cannot match anything, no matter how good the ranking is. Improving ranking cannot move these numbers; only indexing more content can.

## Suggested direction

Candidates, roughly cheapest-first:

1. **Index comments and docstrings.** #44 already covers comment search, so this may partly land there — worth checking for overlap before doing work twice.
2. **Index nested symbols** (methods, nested functions), not just module-level ones. Note this is a deliberate current design choice — module-level symbols are the file public surface — so it should be additive and ranked lower, not a change to what `symbols` means in the file detail panel.
3. **Index identifiers inside function bodies**, as a last resort — highest index cost and the most likely to hurt precision, so it should be measured, not assumed.

## How to verify any change

#37 shipped a reproducible harness, so this is measurable rather than a matter of opinion:

- re-run the labeled query sets and compare against the 0.211 / 0.326 figures above
- the 4 zero-result queries are the clearest success signal — any of them returning a labeled file is real progress
- watch precision does not regress while recall improves

Note the baseline enumerates **tracked** files only (`git ls-files`), so the numbers are reproducible on a clean checkout.

## Related

- #37 / PR #67 — the measurement this comes from
- #36 — reading path recommendations, which consume these results
- #44 — comment search, likely overlapping with suggestion 1
title: Search recall: index holds only paths, module-level symbols and import names, so some queries return nothing

body:
Pre-existing flake on `main`, found while working on #37. Not introduced by that PR.

## Symptom

`backend/tests/test_e2e_reference_repo.py::test_requests_the_commit_then_the_archive_once` fails intermittently — roughly **2 runs in 10**. It fails in isolation too, so it is not cross-test pollution.

## Cause

`PipelineAnalysisRunner.run` deletes the working directory in a `finally`:

```python
# backend/repolens/pipeline/runner.py:151
finally:
    shutil.rmtree(work_dir, ignore_errors=True)
```

The test asserts that the work root is empty. That assertion races the `rmtree`: the analysis is observed as completed and the test proceeds while cleanup is still in flight, so the directory is sometimes still present when the assertion runs.

`ignore_errors=True` means a partially-failed cleanup is also silent, so the race has no diagnostic trail.

## Why it is worth fixing rather than tolerating

This runs in the `End-to-end (reference repo)` CI job, so roughly one in five pushes can go red for a reason unrelated to the change under review. We have already had PRs where a green/red signal on this job needed interpreting rather than trusting, and a flaky gate trains people to re-run CI instead of reading it.

## Suggested fix

Make the cleanup observable rather than racing it. Options, roughly in order of preference:

1. Have the runner signal that cleanup is done — the test waits on that rather than on analysis status.
2. Have the test poll for the work root to become empty with a short timeout, instead of asserting once.
3. Inject the work-root lifecycle so the test owns cleanup and can assert deterministically.

Simply asserting less is not ideal: the assertion is testing something real — that snapshots do not accumulate on disk.

## Reproduction

Run the single test repeatedly:

```
cd backend && for i in $(seq 1 10); do python -m pytest tests/test_e2e_reference_repo.py::test_requests_the_commit_then_the_archive_once -q || echo "FAILED on run $i"; done
```
title: Flaky: test_requests_the_commit_then_the_archive_once races the pipeline snapshot cleanup

body:
Found while landing #26 (file filtering) alongside the pipeline runner from #30.

## Problem

`PipelineAnalysisRunner._run_stages` gates the filtering stage on *language support only*, before the vendored/generated filter runs:

```python
# backend/repolens/pipeline/runner.py:170
if not any(self._analysis_service.supports(path) for path in snapshot.files):
    raise NoPythonFilesError()

# ...then, five lines later:
analysis = self._analysis_service.analyze_repository(snapshot.root)   # line 175
```

`supports(path)` only asks "is this a `.py`/`.pyi` file an analyzer can handle". It is evaluated over **every** file in the snapshot, including vendored and generated ones. The exclusion filter added in #26 is applied later, inside `analyze_repository`.

So for a repository whose only Python lives in `vendor/`, `third_party/`, `build/`, `node_modules/`, or an `.egg-info` directory:

1. Line 170 passes — those files *are* Python, so `NoPythonFilesError` is not raised.
2. Line 175 filters them all out as vendored/generated.
3. The analysis reaches `complete_analysis` with **zero analyzed files** and status `completed`.

## Impact

The user gets an apparently successful analysis with an empty file explorer and an empty dependency map, rather than the clear `NO_PYTHON_FILES` error that already exists for this situation:

> This repository has no Python files to analyze.
> *Hint:* RepoLens currently supports Python repositories only.

A silent empty success is the worst of the available outcomes — there is nothing on screen explaining why.

## Suggested fix

Evaluate the gate against the set of files that will actually be analyzed, i.e. after exclusion, rather than against raw `snapshot.files`. Either move the check after filtering, or have the filter report its analyzable set and gate on that. The existing `NoPythonFilesError` is probably still the right error, though it may deserve a distinct code or hint for "all Python was excluded as vendored/generated" versus "no Python at all" — those are different things to tell a user.

## Notes

- `backend/README.md:390` documents the intended behaviour as "**filtering**: fails with `NO_PYTHON_FILES` if no file has an analyzer", which is what the code does — the gap is that "has an analyzer" and "will be analyzed" diverged once filtering landed.
- Deliberately left untouched by the #26 PR, as `runner.py` was out of that PR scope.
- Practical consequence worth knowing: this is a live demo hazard. Demoing a repo whose Python is all vendored shows an empty, successful-looking analysis.
title: Repos whose only Python is vendored or generated complete with zero analyzed files instead of an error
